entities.name: Adalbert Boros
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Adalbert Boros (1927–1996) was a Hungarian Franciscan friar and theologian whose work on eschatology — the theology of last things, death, and the afterlife — made him one of the most influential Catholic theologians of the post-Vatican II period. Born in Hungary, he joined the Franciscan Order and eventually served as a professor of theology, producing work that engaged deeply with the existential dimensions of Christian faith.

His most significant work, 'The Moment of Death' ('Mysterium Mortis,' 1962), proposed the controversial hypothesis that death is not merely the end of life but the moment of the most fundamental personal decision — the 'final option' in which the soul, freed from the limitations of earthly existence, encounters God directly and makes its definitive choice for or against divine love. This thesis engaged both Catholic systematic theology and existentialist philosophy, particularly the work of Heidegger.

Boros's theology was part of the broader Catholic theological renewal that Vatican II (1962–1965) both encouraged and expressed. His engagement with existentialist philosophy and his attempt to re-express traditional eschatological categories in terms accessible to modern consciousness contributed to the post-conciliar theological project of relating Christian faith to contemporary experience. His work was translated into multiple languages and influenced Catholic eschatology for a generation.
